claim: Impaired angiogenesis is a hallmark of metabolically dysfunctional adipose tissue in obesity.
source: Impaired angiogenesis is a hallmark of metabolically dysfunctional adipose tissue in obesity.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Induced endothelial-specific depletion of FoxO1 in male mice led to increased vascular density in adipose tissue.
source: Here, we demonstrate that induced endothelial-specific depletion of the transcription factor Forkhead Box O1 (FoxO1) in male mice led to increased vascular density in adipose tissue.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Upon high-fat diet feeding, endothelial cell FoxO1-deficient mice exhibited greater vascular remodeling in the visceral adipose depot.
source: Upon high-fat diet feeding, endothelial cell FoxO1-deficient mice exhibited even greater vascular remodeling in the visceral adipose depot, which was paralleled with a healthier adipose tissue expansion, higher glucose tolerance and lower fasting glycemia concomitant with enhanced lactate levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Endothelial cell FoxO1-deficient mice on high-fat diet exhibited healthier adipose tissue expansion.
source: Upon high-fat diet feeding, endothelial cell FoxO1-deficient mice exhibited even greater vascular remodeling in the visceral adipose depot, which was paralleled with a healthier adipose tissue expansion, higher glucose tolerance and lower fasting glycemia concomitant with enhanced lactate levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Endothelial cell FoxO1-deficient mice on high-fat diet exhibited higher glucose tolerance.
source: Upon high-fat diet feeding, endothelial cell FoxO1-deficient mice exhibited even greater vascular remodeling in the visceral adipose depot, which was paralleled with a healthier adipose tissue expansion, higher glucose tolerance and lower fasting glycemia concomitant with enhanced lactate levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Endothelial cell FoxO1-deficient mice on high-fat diet exhibited lower fasting glycemia.
source: Upon high-fat diet feeding, endothelial cell FoxO1-deficient mice exhibited even greater vascular remodeling in the visceral adipose depot, which was paralleled with a healthier adipose tissue expansion, higher glucose tolerance and lower fasting glycemia concomitant with enhanced lactate levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Endothelial cell FoxO1-deficient mice on high-fat diet exhibited enhanced lactate levels.
source: Upon high-fat diet feeding, endothelial cell FoxO1-deficient mice exhibited even greater vascular remodeling in the visceral adipose depot, which was paralleled with a healthier adipose tissue expansion, higher glucose tolerance and lower fasting glycemia concomitant with enhanced lactate levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: FoxO1 depletion increased endothelial proliferative and glycolytic capacities by upregulating the expression of glycolytic markers.
source: Mechanistically, FoxO1 depletion increased endothelial proliferative and glycolytic capacities by upregulating the expression of glycolytic markers, which may account for the improvements at the tissue level ultimately impacting whole-body glucose metabolism.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Upregulation of glycolytic markers by FoxO1 depletion may account for improvements at the tissue level ultimately impacting whole-body glucose metabolism.
source: Mechanistically, FoxO1 depletion increased endothelial proliferative and glycolytic capacities by upregulating the expression of glycolytic markers, which may account for the improvements at the tissue level ultimately impacting whole-body glucose metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanistic findings.

claim: FoxO1 plays a pivotal role in controlling endothelial metabolic and angiogenic adaptations in response to high-fat diet.
source: Altogether, these findings reveal the pivotal role of FoxO1 in controlling endothelial metabolic and angiogenic adaptations in response to high-fat diet and a contribution of the endothelium to whole-body energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The endothelium contributes to whole-body energy homeostasis.
source: Altogether, these findings reveal the pivotal role of FoxO1 in controlling endothelial metabolic and angiogenic adaptations in response to high-fat diet and a contribution of the endothelium to whole-body energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Obesity is a growing problem worldwide.
source: Obesity is a growing problem worldwide (Moller and Kaufman, 2005; Tchernof and Després, 2013) and thus an urgent need exists to identify molecular processes and signaling pathways that may serve as novel therapeutic targets to hinder obesity-induced pathologies.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The dysfunction of adipose tissue plays a central role in the development of peripheral tissue metabolic disturbances.
source: Although the underlying causes of obesity-related complications are multifactorial, the dysfunction of adipose tissue plays a central role in the development of peripheral tissue metabolic disturbances, ultimately reflecting systemically in dyslipidemia, insulin resistance and hyperglycemia (Moller and Kaufman, 2005; Fuster et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Adipose tissue dysfunction ultimately reflects systemically in dyslipidemia, insulin resistance and hyperglycemia.
source: Although the underlying causes of obesity-related complications are multifactorial, the dysfunction of adipose tissue plays a central role in the development of peripheral tissue metabolic disturbances, ultimately reflecting systemically in dyslipidemia, insulin resistance and hyperglycemia (Moller and Kaufman, 2005; Fuster et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: During expansion of visceral adipose tissue, impaired vascular remodeling promotes hypoxia, inflammation, and fibrosis.
source: During expansion of visceral adipose tissue, impaired vascular remodeling promotes hypoxia, inflammation, and fibrosis (Corvera and Gealekman, 2014; Fuster et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Forced stimulation of vascular growth in adipose tissue of obese rodents improves adipose tissue function.
source: Conversely, forced stimulation of vascular growth in adipose tissue of obese rodents improves adipose tissue function (Sun et al., 2012; Robciuc et al., 2016; Seki et al., 2018), counteracting obesity-related metabolic disorders (Sung et al., 2013; Seki et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Forced stimulation of vascular growth in adipose tissue of obese rodents counteracts obesity-related metabolic disorders.
source: Conversely, forced stimulation of vascular growth in adipose tissue of obese rodents improves adipose tissue function (Sun et al., 2012; Robciuc et al., 2016; Seki et al., 2018), counteracting obesity-related metabolic disorders (Sung et al., 2013; Seki et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FoxO1 signaling is essential to the homeostasis of EC and restricts vascular growth.
source: Forkhead Box O1 (FoxO1) signaling is essential to the homeostasis of EC and restricts vascular growth (Wilhelm et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: FoxO1 is a gatekeeper of EC metabolism.
source: In addition to the control of angiogenesis-related genes (Potente et al., 2005; Paik et al., 2007; Milkiewicz et al., 2011; Roudier et al., 2013; Wilhelm et al., 2016), FoxO1 is a gatekeeper of EC metabolism; its overexpression reduces the metabolic rate of EC and enforces a state of endothelial quiescence (Wilhelm et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FoxO1 overexpression reduces the metabolic rate of EC and enforces a state of endothelial quiescence.
source: In addition to the control of angiogenesis-related genes (Potente et al., 2005; Paik et al., 2007; Milkiewicz et al., 2011; Roudier et al., 2013; Wilhelm et al., 2016), FoxO1 is a gatekeeper of EC metabolism; its overexpression reduces the metabolic rate of EC and enforces a state of endothelial quiescence (Wilhelm et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The switch from a quiescent to an angiogenic phenotype requires a coordinated increase in EC metabolic activity.
source: Thus, this transcription factor is one of the major regulators of angiogenic capacity, since the switch from a quiescent to an angiogenic phenotype requires a coordinated increase in EC metabolic activity to meet the higher demand for energy and biomass production associated with proliferation and migration (De Bock et al., 2013; Schoors et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FoxO1 protein levels were elevated in capillaries from skeletal muscle of mice fed a high-fat diet.
source: For instance, FoxO1 protein levels were elevated in capillaries from skeletal muscle of mice fed a high-fat diet (Nwadozi et al., 2016) and the activity of endothelial FoxO1 correlated with adipose insulin resistance of obese subjects (Karki et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The activity of endothelial FoxO1 correlated with adipose insulin resistance of obese subjects.
source: For instance, FoxO1 protein levels were elevated in capillaries from skeletal muscle of mice fed a high-fat diet (Nwadozi et al., 2016) and the activity of endothelial FoxO1 correlated with adipose insulin resistance of obese subjects (Karki et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In vitro conditions that mimic hyperglycemia and insulin resistance increase FoxO1 protein and activity in EC.
source: Additionally, in vitro conditions that mimic hyperglycemia and insulin resistance increase FoxO1 protein and activity in EC (Tanaka et al., 2009; Nwadozi et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Foxo1 transcript level was decreased by 50% in microvascular EC of EC-FoxO1 KD mice relative to control littermates 8 weeks after the administration of tamoxifen.
source: Consequently, Foxo1 transcript level, as measured by qPCR, was decreased by 50% in microvascular EC of EC-FoxO1 KD mice relative to control littermates 8 weeks after the administration of tamoxifen, confirming effective and stable Foxo1 depletion in these cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Foxo3 mRNA expression was unaltered in microvascular EC of EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: Of note, Foxo3 mRNA expression was unaltered in microvascular EC (Figure 1B), demonstrating a lack of compensation by this FoxO family member in response to the depletion of Foxo1.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No significant changes in Foxo1 mRNA levels were detected in CD16/CD32+ immune cells from white adipose tissue of EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: Moreover, consistent with the previously described absence of Pdgfb-Cre activity within macrophages (Claxton et al., 2008), no significant changes in Foxo1 mRNA levels were detected in CD16/CD32+ immune cells from white adipose tissue (Figure 1C), indicating that Cre-mediated recombination did not occur in these stromal cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 1C, supported by citation.

claim: Protein levels of FoxO1 were diminished by 70% in capillary fragments from skeletal muscle of EC-FoxO1 KD mice compared to control littermates 6 weeks after the administration of tamoxifen.
source: In agreement with the lower mRNA levels observed in microvascular ECs from adipose tissue, protein levels of FoxO1 were diminished by 70% in capillary fragments from skeletal muscle of EC-FoxO1 KD mice compared to control littermates 6 weeks after the administration of tamoxifen (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: EC-FoxO1 KD mice maintained on a normal chow diet for 16 weeks exhibited no gross abnormalities.
source: EC-FoxO1 KD mice maintained on a normal chow (NC) diet for 16 weeks exhibited no gross abnormalities and similar body weight gain compared to control counterparts (8.32 ± 1.3 vs. 7.75 ± 1.17 g, n = 6/group), but significantly increased mRNA levels of the EC marker Pecam1 in eWAT (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: EC-FoxO1 KD mice maintained on a normal chow diet for 16 weeks exhibited similar body weight gain compared to control counterparts.
source: EC-FoxO1 KD mice maintained on a normal chow (NC) diet for 16 weeks exhibited no gross abnormalities and similar body weight gain compared to control counterparts (8.32 ± 1.3 vs. 7.75 ± 1.17 g, n = 6/group), but significantly increased mRNA levels of the EC marker Pecam1 in eWAT (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: EC-FoxO1 KD mice maintained on a normal chow diet for 16 weeks exhibited significantly increased mRNA levels of the EC marker Pecam1 in eWAT.
source: EC-FoxO1 KD mice maintained on a normal chow (NC) diet for 16 weeks exhibited no gross abnormalities and similar body weight gain compared to control counterparts (8.32 ± 1.3 vs. 7.75 ± 1.17 g, n = 6/group), but significantly increased mRNA levels of the EC marker Pecam1 in eWAT (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The vascular density of visceral adipose tissue from EC-FoxO1 KD mice on normal chow diet was significantly higher than control mice.
source: When blood vessels were visualized by whole-mount staining with G. simplicifolia lectin, it was evident that the vascular density of visceral adipose tissue from EC-FoxO1 KD mice (Figure 2B–C) was significantly higher.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: EC-FoxO1 depletion did not alter the number of vessel branch points in normal chow fed mice.
source: EC-FoxO1 depletion did not alter the number of vessel branch points (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Vessels in the adipose of EC-FoxO1 KD mice on normal chow diet were significantly enlarged, showing increased vessel diameter, compared to control littermates.
source: On the other hand, vessels in the adipose of EC-FoxO1 KD mice were significantly enlarged, showing increased vessel diameter, compared to control littermates (Figure 2E), which was consistent with the reported influence of EC-Foxo1 depletion in vascular development in retinas (Wilhelm et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 2E, with citation to prior literature.

claim: No difference in the expression of Pecam1 was detected in skeletal muscle and liver of normal chow fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: No difference in the expression of Pecam1 was detected in other assessed tissues, such as skeletal muscle and liver (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: EC-FoxO1 depletion resulted in higher Pecam1 mRNA levels in multiple adipose tissue depots of HF-fed mice: eWAT, subcutaneous and brown adipose tissue.
source: Gene expression analysis indicated that EC-FoxO1 depletion resulted in higher Pecam1 mRNA levels in multiple adipose tissue depots: eWAT, subcutaneous and brown adipose tissue (BAT, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Transcript levels of von Willebrand factor (Vwf) and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (Nos3) were elevated in the eWAT of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: In line therewith, transcript levels of other EC markers, von Willebrand factor (Vwf) and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (Nos3) were elevated in the eWAT of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Whole-mount staining of adipose tissue revealed remarkable increases in vascular area and number of vessel branch points in the eWAT of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: Whole-mount staining of adipose tissue revealed remarkable increases in vascular area and number of vessel branch points in the eWAT of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Capillary number per adipocyte (capillary to adipocyte ratio) was significantly higher in eWAT of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: Consistently, quantitative histological analysis showed that capillary number per adipocyte (capillary to adipocyte ratio) was significantly higher in eWAT of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice, further validating the greater microvascular content in eWAT of these mice compared to HF-fed control counterparts (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: EC-FoxO1 depletion led to significant capillary enlargement in eWAT of HF-fed mice.
source: Furthermore, EC-FoxO1 depletion led to significant capillary enlargement in eWAT (Figure 3H–I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: The increase of vessel diameter in HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice was greater than observed in NC-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice (1.8 vs. 1.3-fold increase).
source: Of note, the increase of vessel diameter in HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice was greater than observed in NC-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice (1.8 vs. 1.3-fold increase), suggesting that the enlargement of capillaries promoted by EC-FoxO1 depletion is exacerbated by HF feeding.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the study's experimental data with speculative interpretation.

claim: EC-FoxO1 depletion did not change transcript levels of Pecam1 in the liver of HF-fed mice.
source: Subsequent gene expression analysis showed that EC-FoxO1 depletion did not change transcript levels of Pecam1 in the liver (corresponding with the lack of Cre recombination in this organ) but did upregulate its expression in skeletal muscle, suggesting that under the stimulus of HF diet, EC-FoxO1 depletion also induces microvascular remodeling in this tissue (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EC-FoxO1 depletion upregulated Pecam1 expression in skeletal muscle of HF-fed mice.
source: Subsequent gene expression analysis showed that EC-FoxO1 depletion did not change transcript levels of Pecam1 in the liver (corresponding with the lack of Cre recombination in this organ) but did upregulate its expression in skeletal muscle, suggesting that under the stimulus of HF diet, EC-FoxO1 depletion also induces microvascular remodeling in this tissue (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 4A with speculative interpretation.

claim: Skeletal muscle of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed a trend towards higher capillary:fiber ratio (p = 0.06) compared to control mice.
source: Skeletal muscle of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed a trend towards higher capillary:fiber ratio (p = 0.06) compared to control mice (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy revealed increased capillary endothelial cross-sectional area and capillary lumen diameters in skeletal muscle of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: Transmission electron microscopy revealed increased capillary endothelial cross-sectional area and capillary lumen diameters in skeletal muscle of EC-FoxO1 KD mice, demonstrating a modest expansion of the size of individual capillaries (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice showed only a trend towards reduced body weight gain (p = 0.06).
source: Although HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice showed only a trend towards reduced body weight gain (p = 0.06), these mice displayed less fat accumulation, showing lower trunk fat content, smaller retroperitoneal (rWAT) and subcutaneous fat pads compared to control mice (Figure 5A–C and Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C and Table 1.

claim: HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed less fat accumulation, showing lower trunk fat content, smaller retroperitoneal (rWAT) and subcutaneous fat pads compared to control mice.
source: Although HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice showed only a trend towards reduced body weight gain (p = 0.06), these mice displayed less fat accumulation, showing lower trunk fat content, smaller retroperitoneal (rWAT) and subcutaneous fat pads compared to control mice (Figure 5A–C and Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C and Table 1.

claim: HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed lower fed levels of serum triglycerides and glycerol.
source: HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice also displayed lower fed levels of serum triglycerides and glycerol, and less hepatic lipid accumulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D), suggesting an improvement in the capacity to handle dietary nutrient excess in these mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D with speculative interpretation.

claim: HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed less hepatic lipid accumulation.
source: HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice also displayed lower fed levels of serum triglycerides and glycerol, and less hepatic lipid accumulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D), suggesting an improvement in the capacity to handle dietary nutrient excess in these mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D with speculative interpretation.

claim: Adipocytes from HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice were smaller-sized and generally spherical, whereas adipocytes from HF-fed control mice were large with irregular polygonal shapes.
source: Moreover, histological analysis revealed that increased vascular growth in adipose tissue of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice was associated with smaller-sized and generally spherical adipocytes, whereas adipocytes from HF-fed control mice were large with irregular polygonal shapes (Figure 5D–E), which was previously related to cellular stress (Giordano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5D-E with citation to prior literature.

claim: Adipocytes from EC-FoxO1 KD mice retained a unilocular structure.
source: Of note, adipocytes from EC-FoxO1 KD mice retained a unilocular structure (Figure 5D) rather than the hallmark multilocular morphology of brown fat.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No change in the mRNA levels of browning markers Ucp1 and Prdm16 was detected with EC-FoxO1 depletion.
source: Furthermore, no change in the mRNA levels of browning markers Ucp1 and Prdm16 (Figure 5F) was detected with EC-FoxO1 depletion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: No difference in mitochondrial protein content of eWAT was observed with EC-FoxO1 depletion.
source: Correspondingly, we did not observe any difference in mitochondrial protein content of eWAT nor in ADP-stimulated respiration through either Complex I (pyruvate/malate, glutamate) or Complex II (succinate) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: No difference in ADP-stimulated respiration through either Complex I or Complex II was observed in eWAT with EC-FoxO1 depletion.
source: Correspondingly, we did not observe any difference in mitochondrial protein content of eWAT nor in ADP-stimulated respiration through either Complex I (pyruvate/malate, glutamate) or Complex II (succinate) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Isoproterenol-stimulated phosphorylation of the hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) was unaffected by EC-FoxO1 depletion.
source: Isoproterenol-stimulated phosphorylation of the hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) was unaffected (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–E), indicating that EC-FoxO1 depletion did not impact the adipose tissue sensitivity to lipolytic stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–E with interpretation.

claim: eWAT from HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed enhanced Akt phosphorylation in response to insulin.
source: In contrast, and consistent with an improved function, eWAT from HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed enhanced Akt phosphorylation in response to insulin (Figure 5G–H), which was accompanied by higher Adiponectin mRNA levels and concomitant lower Leptin expression (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: eWAT from HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice showed higher Adiponectin mRNA levels and concomitant lower Leptin expression.
source: In contrast, and consistent with an improved function, eWAT from HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed enhanced Akt phosphorylation in response to insulin (Figure 5G–H), which was accompanied by higher Adiponectin mRNA levels and concomitant lower Leptin expression (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The transcripts levels of Vegfa and Apelin were higher in eWAT from HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: Notably, the transcripts levels of Vegfa and Apelin were also higher in eWAT from HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice (Figure 5J), providing evidence that the improvements in adipose phenotype include a more pro-angiogenic adipose tissue microenvironment.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 5J with interpretation.

claim: EC-FoxO1 KD mice exhibited reduced VO2 during the dark cycle.
source: Surprisingly, EC-FoxO1 KD mice exhibited reduced VO2 and increased RER during the dark cycle (Figure 6A,C) with equivalent CO2 production and activity levels compared to control mice (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: EC-FoxO1 KD mice exhibited increased RER during the dark cycle.
source: Surprisingly, EC-FoxO1 KD mice exhibited reduced VO2 and increased RER during the dark cycle (Figure 6A,C) with equivalent CO2 production and activity levels compared to control mice (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: EC-FoxO1 KD mice exhibited equivalent CO2 production and activity levels compared to control mice.
source: Surprisingly, EC-FoxO1 KD mice exhibited reduced VO2 and increased RER during the dark cycle (Figure 6A,C) with equivalent CO2 production and activity levels compared to control mice (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: EC-FoxO1 KD mice increased oxidation of carbohydrate relative to fatty acid as an energy substrate.
source: These data unexpectedly indicated that EC-FoxO1 KD mice increased oxidation of carbohydrate relative to fatty acid as an energy substrate, suggesting that EC-FoxO1 depletion shifted whole-body energy homeostasis towards glucose oxidation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the metabolic data with speculative reasoning.

claim: HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed more rapid glucose clearance from the blood during glucose tolerance tests.
source: Consistent with these findings, HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed more rapid glucose clearance from the blood during glucose tolerance tests (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Higher glucose tolerance in HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice was not associated with altered whole-body insulin sensitivity, based on insulin tolerance tests.
source: However, higher glucose tolerance was not associated with altered whole-body insulin sensitivity, based on insulin tolerance tests (ITT) (Figure 6G–H) or insulin-mediated Akt phosphorylation in the skeletal muscle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 6G-H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: No change in whole-body glucose metabolism was detected in NC-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice compared to control counterparts.
source: Despite the effects on glucose metabolism observed in HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice, no change in whole-body glucose metabolism was detected in NC-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice compared to control counterparts (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Fasting glycemia was significantly lower in HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: Interestingly, fasting glycemia was significantly lower (Figure 6I) whereas serum lactate levels were elevated in HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice compared to their littermates (10.9 ± 0.39 vs. 9.4 ± 0.55 mmol/L, respectively, p = 0.04, n = 7/group).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Serum lactate levels were elevated in HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice compared to their littermates (10.9 ± 0.39 vs. 9.4 ± 0.55 mmol/L, respectively, p = 0.04, n = 7/group).
source: Interestingly, fasting glycemia was significantly lower (Figure 6I) whereas serum lactate levels were elevated in HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice compared to their littermates (10.9 ± 0.39 vs. 9.4 ± 0.55 mmol/L, respectively, p = 0.04, n = 7/group).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: The mRNA levels of most glycolytic genes, with the exception of Pfkfb3, were upregulated in the eWAT from HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice compared to control mice.
source: As anticipated, the mRNA levels of most glycolytic genes, with the exception of Pfkfb3, were upregulated in the eWAT from HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice compared to control mice, (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: mRNA levels of the lactate transporter, monocarboxylate transporter 5, Slc16a4, were increased in eWAT of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: Furthermore, mRNA levels of the lactate transporter, monocarboxylate transporter 5, Slc16a4, were also increased in eWAT of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice (Figure 6K), consistent with an increased glycolytic flux of glucose to lactate in the adipose tissue of these mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 6K with interpretation.

claim: Increased mRNA levels of glycolytic genes Slc2a1, Pfkm and Pfkfb3 were detected in the EC fraction from adipose tissue of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: Consistent with the findings observed with whole adipose tissue, increased mRNA levels of glycolytic genes Slc2a1, Pfkm and Pfkfb3 were detected in the EC fraction from adipose tissue of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: EC freshly isolated from adipose tissue of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed increased glucose uptake than EC from floxed controls.
source: In agreement with higher transcript levels of Slc2a1, EC freshly isolated from adipose tissue of HF-fed EC-FoxO1 KD mice displayed increased glucose uptake than EC from floxed controls (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Rates of glucose consumption and lactate production were higher in EC with FoxO1 depletion compared to control cells.
source: Moreover, rates of glucose consumption and lactate production were higher in EC with FoxO1 depletion compared to control cells (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: Elevated Mki67 mRNA was observed in the EC fraction from EC-FoxO1 KD mice.
source: Additionally, we observed elevated Mki67 mRNA in the EC fraction from EC-FoxO1 KD mice, indicating that an enhanced proliferative state coincides with the glycolytic activity of these EC (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 7F with interpretation.

claim: High-glucose significantly increased FoxO1 protein levels in cultured EC.
source: As expected, high-glucose significantly increased FoxO1 protein levels in cultured EC (Figure 8A–B) and provoked changes in established FoxO1 target genes Cdkn1b (p27) and Ccnd1 (cyclin D1) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B) that are involved in cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: High-glucose conditions lowered the mRNA levels of glycolytic pathway components Slc2a1, Hk2, and Pfkfb3 in cultured EC.
source: Consistent with increased FoxO1 levels and activity, high-glucose conditions also lowered the mRNA levels of glycolytic pathway components Slc2a1, Hk2, and Pfkfb3 (Figure 8C–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 8C-E.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of FoxO1 significantly reversed the high-glucose-induced reduction of Slc2a1, Hk2, and Pfkfb3 genes.
source: Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of FoxO1 significantly reversed the high-glucose-induced reduction of each of these genes (Figure 8C–E), which correlated with elevated protein levels of HK2 and PFKFB3 (Figure 8F–I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data shown in Figure 8C-I.

claim: Treatment with FoxO1 inhibitor AS1842856 increased cellular glucose uptake and consumption in microvascular ECs.
